text.en: Find the notes of line 1: each one waits until you're on it.
It was first printed in 1784, in Edward Jones's Musical and Poetical Relicks of the Welsh Bards, as a song for voice and harp with five variations on the accompaniment.

source.en: Hymnology Archive, "God That Madest Earth and Heaven" (AR HYD Y NOS)

text.en: Hear line 1, then sing it back.
Hear line 2, then sing it back.
Line 3 is the tune of line 1 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Line 4 is line 2 again. Sing it with the guide.
Now lines 1 to 4 joined, with the guide.
Hear line 5, then sing it back.
Hear line 6, then sing it back.
Line 7 is the tune of line 1 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Hear line 8, then sing it back.
Now lines 5 to 8 joined, with the guide.
The whole song, with the guide.
Sing your part with the other parts, and the guide with you. Hold your line while the others move.
The guide drops out: your part with the others only. Give me my note plays your first note quietly.
Once more on your own, from the top.
Record the tune of All Through the Night in Sing, with the other parts playing.
Hymnals list its metre as 8.4.8.4.8.8.8.4: long lines answered by a short one. In the English song that short line is the title, and it waits out three long lines before closing.

source.en: Hymnary.org, "AR HYD Y NOS" (tune information); Wikisource, "Ar Hyd y Nos (Boulton/Maynard)"
